questions: Did the eye-movement problem and the difficulty walking on your heels begin during the same illness or event?
Did these symptoms begin suddenly, over minutes to hours?
Have the symptoms been getting progressively worse?
Is the limitation of eye abduction present in only one eye?
Is the difficulty walking on your heels present in both feet?
Do you have double vision?
Do you have a new or severe headache?
Do you have pain around or behind either eye?
Have you noticed loss of vision?
Have you had facial weakness or facial numbness?
Have you had weakness in an arm or in another part of a leg?
Have you had numbness or tingling in your legs or feet?
Have you had back pain radiating down either leg?
Have you had difficulty controlling your bladder or bowels?
Have you had difficulty speaking or swallowing?
Have you had vertigo, imbalance, or difficulty coordinating your movements?
Have you had weakness that is worse later in the day or after exertion?
Have you recently had a respiratory or diarrheal illness?
Have you had fever or unexplained weight loss?
Do you have diabetes?
Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or a history of vascular disease?
Do you have a history of cancer?
Have you recently had head, neck, or back trauma?
Have you ever had similar neurological symptoms before?
Are you taking any medication that suppresses your immune system?

results: 1. Comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic examination with ocular alignment, ductions/versions, saccades, pupils, visual fields, funduscopy, and fatigability testing
fundoscopy: normal
sustained upgaze fatigability test: no fatigable droop
ocular motility examination: bilateral limitation of abduction, worse on the right, with diplopia in all directions
pupil examination (size, light reaction): equal and reactive
cover test / ocular alignment: orthophoric
2. Complete neurological examination including cranial nerves, strength, reflexes, sensation, gait, and focused assessment of dorsiflexion and ankle eversion
cranial nerve examination: bilateral abduction limitation, worse on the right, with diplopia in all directions
limb strength (MRC) examination: mild distal limb weakness
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: reduced or absent reflexes; flexor plantar responses
sensory examination (pinprick, vibration, proprioception): distal loss of vibration and proprioception
3. MRI of the brain and orbits with and without gadolinium, including the cavernous sinuses and brainstem
MRI orbits: normal extraocular muscles, no mass
MRI brain with contrast: bilateral contrast enhancement and THICKENING of cranial nerves III through XII
4. MR venography of the intracranial venous sinuses
not performed / not available
5. Nerve-conduction studies and needle electromyography of both lower limbs
nerve conduction studies: demyelinating sensorimotor neuropathy
needle electromyography: chronic neurogenic changes
6. Serum acetylcholine-receptor antibodies and MuSK antibodies
anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies: negative
anti-MuSK antibodies: negative
7. Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver profile, fasting glucose, HbA1c, thyroid function tests, vitamin B12, ESR, and CRP
full blood count: normal
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
liver function tests: normal
glucose / HbA1c: normal
vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid: normal
ESR / CRP: normal - against giant cell arteritis
8. Serum Lyme disease and syphilis serology
HIV and syphilis serology: normal
9. Lumbar puncture with opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, cytology, and appropriate infectious studies
lumbar puncture / CSF: protein mildly raised at 73 mg/dL
CSF opening pressure: normal
CSF cell count and differential: normal
CSF protein: mildly raised at 73 mg/dL
CSF glucose: normal
CSF cytology and flow cytometry: normal
CSF culture and viral PCR: normal
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Guillain–Barré syndrome, acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with multiple cranial-nerve involvement (polyneuritis cranialis variant), presumed autoimmune

ALTERNATIVE 1: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with cranial-nerve involvement

ALTERNATIVE 2: Neurolymphomatosis from occult lymphoma

ALTERNATIVE 3: Neurosarcoidosis causing hypertrophic cranial polyneuropathy
